lessons.title: Cancer biology and the cancers you will actually meet
lessons.body:
## Two kinds of broken gene

Cancer is a disease of accumulated mutations in two opposite kinds of gene.

An **oncogene** is an accelerator stuck on. One damaged copy is enough, because gaining function needs only one hit. Examples: `RAS` in colon and pancreatic cancer, `HER2` in breast cancer, `BCR-ABL` in chronic myeloid leukemia, `EGFR` in lung adenocarcinoma.

A **tumor suppressor** is a brake that has failed. Both copies must be lost, which is why these cancers run in families: an inherited first hit means only one more is needed. Examples: `p53`, the most commonly mutated gene in human cancer, `RB` in retinoblastoma, `BRCA1` and `BRCA2` in breast and ovarian cancer, `APC` in colon cancer.

## The capabilities a cell must acquire

A malignant cell has to solve several problems, and each solution is a drug target.

1. Grow without being told to, and ignore signals to stop.
2. Resist apoptosis, usually by disabling `p53`.
3. Divide without limit by reactivating telomerase.
4. Build its own blood supply through angiogenesis, which bevacizumab attacks.
5. Hide from immune cells, often by displaying PD-L1, which checkpoint inhibitors block.
6. Invade through the basement membrane and metastasize.

> **Key:** Progression is stepwise and takes years: normal tissue, then hyperplasia, then dysplasia, then carcinoma in place, then invasion. Screening exists because every step before invasion is either reversible or curable, and the colon is the model — an adenomatous polyp removed at colonoscopy is a cancer that never happens.

## Where each cancer goes

Metastasis is not random. Blood from the colon drains through the portal vein, so colon cancer seeds the liver. Prostate cancer spreads through vertebral veins to bone and makes dense, bone-building lesions. Lung cancer goes to brain, bone, adrenal, and liver. Breast cancer goes to bone, lung, liver, and brain.

| Cancer | Who | Presentation that matters |
|---|---|---|
| Lung | smokers; small cell and non-small cell | cough, weight loss, hemoptysis; small cell causes SIADH and squamous cell causes hypercalcemia through PTH-related peptide |
| Breast | women, `BRCA` carriers | painless firm mass, skin dimpling, nipple change; typed by estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors |
| Colorectal | age over `45`, family history, inflammatory bowel disease | right-sided bleeds silently and causes iron deficiency anemia, left-sided obstructs |
| Prostate | older men | often silent; bone pain and back pain from vertebral metastases |
| Pancreatic | smokers, chronic pancreatitis | painless jaundice with a palpable non-tender gallbladder, weight loss, new diabetes |
| Cervical | HPV types `16` and `18` | abnormal bleeding; almost entirely preventable by vaccination and screening |

> **Trap:** Iron deficiency anemia in a man or a postmenopausal woman is colon cancer until a colonoscopy says otherwise. The tumor bleeds a teaspoon a day, which is invisible in the toilet and obvious in the ferritin.

## Paraneoplastic syndromes

Some tumors secrete hormones, which is why the first sign of cancer can be a chemistry panel. Small cell lung cancer makes antidiuretic hormone (hyponatremia) or ACTH (Cushing syndrome). Squamous cell cancers make PTH-related peptide (hypercalcemia). Myeloma causes hypercalcemia by eating bone directly. Lambert-Eaton syndrome, weakness that improves with repeated effort, is an antibody attack triggered by small cell lung cancer.

## Stage and grade are different questions

**Grade** describes how abnormal the cells look under the microscope. **Stage** describes how far the disease has travelled, using TNM: tumor size, nodes involved, metastasis present. Stage drives prognosis and treatment far more than grade does, which is why a small, ugly tumor may be curable and a large, bland one with liver metastases is not.
keyPoints: Oncogenes are accelerators needing one hit; tumor suppressors are brakes needing both copies lost, which is why they run in families.
Progression is normal, hyperplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in place, invasion — screening works because every earlier step is treatable.
Metastasis follows drainage: colon to liver by the portal vein, prostate to bone, lung to brain, bone, adrenal, and liver.
Iron deficiency anemia in a man or postmenopausal woman is colon cancer until colonoscopy proves otherwise.
Paraneoplastic syndromes mean a chemistry panel can be the first sign: SIADH and ectopic ACTH from small cell, hypercalcemia from squamous cell.

checks.q: A 64-year-old man has a hemoglobin of 9.1 g/dL, a ferritin of 8 ng/mL, and no visible bleeding. What is the required next step?
choices: Start oral iron and recheck in 3 months
Reassure; this is common at his age
checks.why: Iron deficiency in a man means chronic occult blood loss, and the colon is the source until proven otherwise. Right-sided colon cancers bleed slowly and silently. Iron alone treats the number and ignores the cause, and B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic, not microcytic, anemia.

checks.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer has a sodium of 118 mEq/L with concentrated urine and normal volume status. What is the mechanism?
choices: Tumor secretion of antidiuretic hormone causing water retention
Loss of sodium through the kidney from tumor invasion
checks.why: Small cell lung cancer classically secretes antidiuretic hormone, producing SIADH: euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine. PTH-related peptide comes from squamous cell cancers and causes hypercalcemia, not hyponatremia.

checks.q: Why do tumor suppressor gene syndromes such as BRCA cluster in families while most oncogene mutations do not?
choices: Tumor suppressors are only found in reproductive tissue
An inherited first hit means only one further mutation is needed to lose both copies
Oncogenes cannot be inherited at all
Tumor suppressor mutations are always present at birth in every cell of every person
checks.why: Tumor suppressors require loss of both copies. Inheriting one damaged copy means every cell already has the first hit, so cancer risk is dramatically higher and appears earlier. Oncogenes need only one hit but that hit is usually acquired somatically.

lessons.title: Autoimmune disease: when the immune system reads self as foreign
lessons.body:
## Tolerance and how it breaks

The immune system learns not to attack the body twice. **Central tolerance** deletes self-reactive lymphocytes as they mature in the thymus and bone marrow. **Peripheral tolerance** catches the escapees with regulatory T cells and by shutting down cells that see an antigen without a danger signal.

Autoimmunity begins when both filters fail. Three mechanisms explain most of it.

- **Molecular mimicry**: a microbe wears a protein that resembles a human one. Streptococcal M protein resembles cardiac myosin, so antibodies made against a sore throat attack the heart valves two weeks later. That is rheumatic fever. Campylobacter surface sugars resemble peripheral nerve myelin, which is how Guillain-Barre syndrome follows gastroenteritis.
- **Cryptic antigen release**: tissue that was never shown to the immune system is exposed by injury or infection.
- **Loss of regulation**: regulatory T cells fail, or a viral infection provides the danger signal that wakes up a self-reactive cell that had been ignored.

Genetics loads the gun, usually through HLA type, and an environmental trigger fires it. Most autoimmune disease is far more common in women.

## The four hypersensitivity types

| Type | Mediator | Timing | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | IgE on mast cells | minutes | anaphylaxis, allergic asthma, hay fever |
| II | antibody against a cell surface | hours to days | immune thrombocytopenia, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Graves disease, myasthenia gravis, Goodpasture |
| III | antigen-antibody complexes deposited in tissue | days | lupus, serum sickness, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis |
| IV | T cells, no antibody | `48-72` hours | contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, transplant rejection |

> **Key:** Type II attacks a specific cell. Type III makes complexes that float and lodge wherever filtration happens, which is why lupus hits kidney, skin, and joints at once. Type IV is the only one with no antibody at all, and it is why a rash appears days after a drug rather than minutes.

## The diseases to recognize

**Lupus** is the model immune complex disease. Antinuclear antibody is sensitive but not specific; anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith are specific. Lupus nephritis drives most of the mortality, and antiphospholipid antibodies paradoxically cause clotting with a prolonged PTT.

**Rheumatoid arthritis** is synovial inflammation that grows an invasive tissue (pannus) which erodes cartilage and bone. Symmetric small joints of hands and feet, morning stiffness lasting more than an hour that improves with use, and anti-CCP antibodies. Osteoarthritis is the opposite pattern: asymmetric, worse with use, brief stiffness, no systemic features.

**Graves disease** is a type II antibody that stimulates rather than destroys the TSH receptor. **Hashimoto thyroiditis** is the destructive version with anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies. **Type 1 diabetes** is T-cell destruction of pancreatic beta cells.

**Myasthenia gravis** is antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, so the signal fades with repetition: ptosis and double vision that worsen through the day and with sustained upward gaze. In a crisis the danger is respiratory muscle failure, and oxygen saturation stays normal until the patient is nearly apneic, so bedside vital capacity and negative inspiratory force are what get measured.

**Giant cell arteritis** is a vasculitis of medium and large arteries in patients over `50`: new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain while chewing, and a markedly raised ESR. Vision loss can be permanent within hours, so steroids are started before the temporal artery biopsy, not after.

> **On shift:** Any patient on chronic steroids, methotrexate, or a biologic has a blunted fever and a muted examination. Infection in these patients looks milder than it is, and that is exactly why it kills them.
keyPoints: Autoimmunity is failed central and peripheral tolerance, usually triggered by molecular mimicry in a genetically primed person.
Type I is IgE in minutes, type II is antibody against a cell, type III is immune complexes, type IV is T cells at 48-72 hours.
Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith are specific for lupus; anti-CCP is specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
Myasthenic crisis is measured with vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, because saturation stays normal until near-apnea.
Giant cell arteritis gets steroids before the biopsy, because vision loss becomes permanent within hours.

checks.q: Two weeks after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis, a child develops a new murmur, migratory arthritis, and fever. What is the mechanism?
choices: Direct bacterial invasion of the heart valve
Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac myosin
checks.why: Rheumatic fever is antibody cross-reaction: M protein resembles cardiac myosin, so antibodies raised against the streptococcus attack the heart. Direct invasion would be endocarditis with positive blood cultures, and IgE and toxins act within minutes to hours, not two weeks.

checks.q: A 34-year-old with myasthenia gravis has worsening weakness and a normal oxygen saturation on room air. What determines the need for intubation?
choices: Forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force trends
checks.why: Neuromuscular respiratory failure is a pump problem; saturation and oxygen tension stay normal until the patient is nearly apneic, so waiting for desaturation means waiting too long. Serial vital capacity and negative inspiratory force detect the decline early. Peak flow measures airway obstruction, not muscle strength.

checks.q: Which hypersensitivity type explains a rash that appears three days after starting an antibiotic?
choices: Type II, antibody against a cell surface
checks.why: A delay of days points to T-cell recruitment, which is type IV; this is the mechanism behind most drug rashes including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Type I reactions occur within minutes, type II targets specific cells such as platelets, and type III produces serum sickness with fever, arthralgia, and rash on a different timeline.

lessons.title: Inherited disease you will meet in the emergency department
lessons.body:
## Four inheritance patterns, recognized by shape

**Autosomal dominant** disease appears in every generation and each child of an affected parent has a `50%` chance. Dominant conditions usually involve structural proteins: Marfan syndrome, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, polycystic kidney disease, Huntington disease, familial hypercholesterolemia, and most congenital long QT syndromes.

**Autosomal recessive** disease skips generations and appears in siblings of unaffected carriers. Recessive conditions usually involve enzymes: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, thalassemia, phenylketonuria.

**X-linked recessive** disease affects males, is passed through unaffected carrier mothers, and never goes father to son: hemophilia A and B, G6PD deficiency, Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

**Mitochondrial** disease passes only from the mother, because sperm contribute no mitochondria.

Two words explain why families do not look identical. **Penetrance** is the fraction of people with the gene who show the disease. **Expressivity** is how severely it shows.

## Sickle cell disease

A single amino acid swap at position `6` of the beta-globin chain produces hemoglobin S. When deoxygenated, hemoglobin S polymerizes into rigid rods that deform the red cell into a crescent. Those cells are stiff, sticky, and short-lived, so the patient has both **vaso-occlusion** and **chronic hemolysis**.

Repeated splenic infarction leaves the patient functionally asplenic by early childhood, so encapsulated organisms become lethal: pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, meningococcus, and Salmonella in bone.

| Crisis | What is happening |
|---|---|
| Vaso-occlusive | microvascular obstruction causing bone and chest pain |
| Acute chest syndrome | new infiltrate plus fever or hypoxia; the leading cause of death |
| Splenic sequestration | blood trapped in the spleen; sudden anemia with a big spleen, in young children |
| Aplastic | parvovirus B19 shuts off red cell production; reticulocyte count falls to zero |
| Stroke | large-vessel occlusion, most common between ages `2` and `10` |

> **Key:** Fever in sickle cell disease is a medical emergency, not a viral illness. A functionally asplenic patient can go from a temperature to overwhelming sepsis in hours, and blood cultures plus ceftriaxone come before anything else.

## Hemophilia

Hemophilia A is missing factor VIII, hemophilia B is missing factor IX. Both are X-linked, both prolong the PTT while leaving the PT and the platelet count normal, and both cause deep bleeding into joints and muscle rather than the petechiae of a platelet problem.

> **Trap:** In a hemophilia patient with a head injury, factor replacement goes in before the CT scan, not after. The imaging does not change the treatment and the delay does.

## Marfan syndrome

A mutation in the fibrillin-1 gene weakens the connective tissue scaffolding of the aorta, the eye, and the lung. Tall stature, long fingers, an arm span greater than height, a lens that dislocates upward, and joint laxity. The aortic root dilates over years and then tears: Marfan patients present with type A aortic dissection at an age when nobody expects it, and with spontaneous pneumothorax.

## The channelopathies

Congenital long QT syndrome is a potassium or sodium channel mutation that delays repolarization. The story is syncope or sudden death during exertion, emotion, or a startling noise such as an alarm clock, plus a family history of young sudden death or of drowning in a strong swimmer. Torsades de pointes is the arrhythmia. Management is avoiding every QT-prolonging drug, beta blockade, and often an implanted defibrillator. Brugada syndrome and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are the other inherited causes of sudden death in the young.

## Two more worth recognizing

**G6PD deficiency** leaves red cells unable to handle oxidative stress, so sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, or fava beans trigger sudden hemolysis with bite cells on the smear.

**Hereditary angioedema** is C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency. Swelling of face, airway, or bowel with no hives and no itch, unresponsive to epinephrine, steroids, and antihistamines, because the mediator is bradykinin rather than histamine.
keyPoints: Dominant conditions damage structural proteins and appear every generation; recessive conditions damage enzymes and skip generations.
Sickle hemoglobin polymerizes when deoxygenated, causing both vaso-occlusion and hemolysis, with functional asplenia by childhood.
Fever in sickle cell disease is an emergency: cultures and ceftriaxone before anything else.
Hemophilia prolongs the PTT with a normal PT and platelet count, and head injury gets factor before imaging.
Marfan syndrome causes type A aortic dissection in young patients; congenital long QT causes syncope with exertion or startle.

checks.q: A 9-year-old with sickle cell disease has a temperature of 38.9 C and looks well. What is the correct approach?
choices: Treat as a viral illness with antipyretics and discharge
Blood cultures and ceftriaxone promptly, because functional asplenia allows rapid overwhelming sepsis
Wait for the white count before deciding
Give a fluid bolus and reassess in 6 hours
checks.why: Repeated splenic infarction leaves these children functionally asplenic, so encapsulated organisms can produce fulminant sepsis within hours. Cultures and an immediate third-generation cephalosporin are standard. A well appearance and a normal white count do not exclude early bacteremia.

checks.q: A 16-year-old boy with hemophilia A falls and strikes his head. He is alert with a normal examination. What happens first?
choices: CT head, then factor VIII if bleeding is seen
Factor VIII replacement immediately, then CT head
checks.why: Intracranial bleeding in hemophilia can be catastrophic and the CT result does not change the need for factor. Replacement goes first and imaging follows. Platelets are normal in hemophilia, so transfusing them does nothing.

checks.q: A tall 24-year-old with long fingers and an upward-dislocated lens has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Type A aortic dissection from Marfan syndrome
checks.why: Fibrillin-1 mutation weakens the aortic media, so Marfan patients dissect decades earlier than the general population. Tearing pain radiating to the back in a young Marfan patient is dissection until excluded. Pneumothorax also occurs in Marfan but causes pleuritic pain and breathlessness rather than tearing pain.

lessons.title: How each common infection actually damages tissue
lessons.body:
## Pneumonia: an alveolus full of the wrong thing

Organisms reach the alveoli by inhalation or micro-aspiration. Neutrophils flood in, capillaries leak, and the air sac fills with exudate. That lung segment is still perfused but no longer ventilated, which is a shunt, and shunt is why a lobar pneumonia makes a patient hypoxemic in a way that extra oxygen only partly fixes.

**Typical** pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae) fills a whole lobe with pus: abrupt fever, rigors, rusty sputum, dense consolidation. **Atypical** pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia, viruses) inflames the interstitium between alveoli instead, producing a dry cough, a patient who looks better than the film, and no response to beta-lactams because Mycoplasma has no cell wall to attack.

Aspiration follows gravity into dependent segments: the right lower lobe when upright, the right upper lobe posterior segment when supine. Complications escalate in order: parapneumonic effusion, then infected effusion (empyema) which must be drained, then lung abscess.

## Urinary tract: an ascending problem

Uropathogenic E. coli carries P fimbriae that grip the urothelium against the flow of urine. Cystitis is surface inflammation of the bladder: burning, frequency, no fever. Once organisms ascend the ureter and invade kidney tissue, it becomes pyelonephritis: fever, flank pain, vomiting, and white blood cell casts in the urine, which prove the infection is in the kidney rather than the bladder.

Obstruction turns infection into an emergency. A stone above an infected kidney creates a closed, pressurized abscess that antibiotics cannot sterilize, and bacteria are forced into the bloodstream. Catheters add a biofilm the immune system cannot reach.

## Meningitis: the damage is the response

Organisms cross into cerebrospinal fluid, a space with almost no resident immune defense, and multiply freely. The immune response that follows is what injures the brain: cytokines break down the blood-brain barrier, fluid leaks into brain tissue (vasogenic edema), intracranial pressure rises, and cerebral perfusion falls.

| Finding | Bacterial | Viral |
|---|---|---|
| Opening pressure | high | normal or slightly high |
| White cells | thousands, neutrophils | tens to hundreds, lymphocytes |
| Glucose | low, under two thirds of serum | normal |
| Protein | high | normal or mildly high |

> **Key:** Dexamethasone is given before or with the first antibiotic because killing bacteria releases a burst of cell wall fragments that intensifies inflammation. Blunting that burst reduces hearing loss and death. Given afterward it is too late to matter.

## Endocarditis: a clot that got infected

Turbulent flow across an abnormal valve strips endothelium, and platelets and fibrin form a sterile clot on the damaged spot. When bacteria pass through the blood they stick to that clot and grow inside it, shielded from neutrophils by layers of fibrin. That is why endocarditis needs weeks of intravenous antibiotics rather than days.

Staphylococcus aureus is aggressive and attacks normal valves; viridans streptococci from the mouth colonize already-damaged ones slowly. Injection drug use seeds the tricuspid valve, sending septic emboli to the lungs. The peripheral signs split into two mechanisms: Janeway lesions are painless and embolic, Osler nodes are painful and immune-complex driven.

## From cellulitis to necrotizing fasciitis

Cellulitis is streptococcal infection spreading through the dermis and superficial lymphatics, which is why the border is indistinct and the limb is uniformly red and warm.

Necrotizing infection travels along the fascial plane instead, thrombosing the small vessels that perforate up to the skin. That single fact explains the whole presentation: the deep tissue is dying while the skin still looks nearly normal, the cutaneous nerves die so the skin becomes numb, and the pain is far worse than the appearance justifies. Gas appears when anaerobes are involved. Antibiotics cannot reach dead, avascular tissue, so surgery is the treatment.

## Sepsis, second pass

Beyond the cytokine storm, three mechanisms explain why septic patients fail to improve with pressure alone. The **glycocalyx**, a sugar layer lining the endothelium, is shed, which makes capillaries leak and platelets stick. The **microcirculation** becomes heterogeneous, so some capillaries are plugged while others shunt blood past tissue, which is why central venous oxygen saturation can be high while cells suffocate. And **mitochondria** themselves stop using oxygen efficiently. Late in sepsis the pendulum swings to immune suppression, and the patient who survived the first week dies of a second infection in the third.
keyPoints: Consolidated lung is perfused but unventilated, which is a shunt, so pneumonia hypoxemia responds poorly to oxygen alone.
White blood cell casts prove the infection is in kidney tissue; obstruction above infection is a drainage emergency.
In meningitis the cytokine response causes the brain injury, which is why dexamethasone precedes the first antibiotic.
Endocarditis begins as a sterile platelet-fibrin clot that bacteria colonize and fibrin then shields from neutrophils.
Necrotizing infection thromboses perforating vessels, producing numb skin and pain out of proportion over dying fascia.

checks.q: A patient with dense right lower lobe consolidation has a saturation of 86% that improves only to 90% on a non-rebreather. What explains this?
choices: Shunt: blood perfuses alveoli that are filled and cannot be ventilated
checks.why: Filled alveoli cannot exchange gas, so blood flowing past them never meets the supplemental oxygen. This is shunt physiology, the form of V/Q mismatch that responds poorly to increasing FiO2. Hypoventilation would raise carbon dioxide and correct readily with oxygen.

checks.q: Why must dexamethasone be given before or with the first antibiotic dose in bacterial meningitis?
choices: It improves antibiotic penetration into cerebrospinal fluid
Bacterial killing releases cell wall fragments that worsen inflammation, and blunting that burst reduces hearing loss and death
It treats the fever, allowing the antibiotic to work
checks.why: Lysing bacteria dump inflammatory fragments into the cerebrospinal fluid, intensifying the cytokine response that damages the brain. Steroids given first blunt that surge. Steroids actually reduce cerebrospinal fluid penetration of vancomycin slightly, and they have nothing to do with allergy.

checks.q: A diabetic patient has a red leg with pain far out of proportion to the appearance, a patch of skin that feels numb, and a rising lactate. What is the diagnosis and the treatment?
choices: Necrotizing fasciitis; emergency surgical debridement with broad antibiotics
checks.why: Pain out of proportion with cutaneous anesthesia reflects thrombosed perforating vessels and dying nerves over infected fascia. Antibiotics cannot penetrate avascular necrotic tissue, so surgery is the definitive treatment. Cellulitis is tender but not anesthetic, and deep vein thrombosis does not cause skin numbness or lactate elevation.

lessons.title: Neurologic pathophysiology: degeneration, demyelination, and pressure
lessons.body:
## The dementias are not one disease

| Type | Mechanism | Recognizable pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Alzheimer | amyloid plaques outside cells and tau tangles inside them, starting in the hippocampus | gradual memory loss first, then language and orientation |
| Vascular | accumulated small infarcts | stepwise decline with focal deficits and vascular risk factors |
| Lewy body | alpha-synuclein deposits | fluctuating attention, detailed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, severe sensitivity to antipsychotics |
| Frontotemporal | frontal and temporal lobe degeneration | personality and behavior change first, often before age `65`, memory relatively spared |

> **Trap:** Never give haloperidol to a patient with Lewy body dementia. The sensitivity is not a mild side effect; it can produce severe rigidity, autonomic instability, and death. Quetiapine is the usual alternative.

Delirium is the one that must not be missed: acute onset, fluctuating course, and inattention, almost always caused by something outside the brain. Dementia is slow and stable from hour to hour; delirium changes within a shift.

## Parkinson disease

Dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra die, taking away the signal that smooths and initiates movement. Symptoms do not appear until roughly `60%` to `80%` of those neurons are gone, which is why the disease is always older than the diagnosis. The retained cells contain alpha-synuclein clumps called Lewy bodies.

The four signs are a resting tremor that disappears with movement, cogwheel rigidity, slowness and poverty of movement, and late postural instability with falls.

Two practical consequences. Levodopa-carbidopa must not be interrupted; abrupt withdrawal can produce a syndrome of rigidity and fever resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome. And dopamine-blocking drugs make Parkinson disease acutely worse, so metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, and haloperidol are avoided in favor of ondansetron and quetiapine.

## Multiple sclerosis

T cells cross into the central nervous system and attack myelin made by oligodendrocytes. Conduction slows or fails along the stripped axon, producing deficits that are separated in space and in time, which is the diagnostic idea.

Characteristic findings: optic neuritis with painful vision loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect; internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a lesion between the eye movement nuclei; an electric shock down the spine on neck flexion; and worsening of old symptoms whenever the patient is hot, from a fever, exercise, or a bath, because warm axons conduct even worse. MRI shows plaques and the cerebrospinal fluid shows oligoclonal bands. An acute relapse is treated with high-dose steroids.

## Migraine

Migraine is a brain excitability disorder, not a vascular spasm. A slow wave of neuronal depolarization followed by suppression creeps across the cortex at about `3 mm` per minute, which is exactly the speed of a visual aura spreading across the field. That wave activates the trigeminal nerve endings around the meningeal vessels, which release calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and other peptides, producing neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, and pain.

Repeated activation sensitizes the system centrally, which is why the scalp hurts to touch and why treatment given late works poorly. Triptans act on serotonin receptors to shut off peptide release; CGRP blockers target the peptide directly. In the emergency department the effective agents are dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, often with diphenhydramine to prevent akathisia, plus ketorolac and fluids. Opioids work badly and make the next migraine harder to treat.

## Pressure in a closed box

The skull holds brain, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid in a fixed volume, so adding anything means displacing something else. Cerebrospinal fluid and venous blood buffer the first additions, which is why intracranial pressure stays nearly flat as a bleed grows, and then rises steeply once the buffers are spent. Small additional volume then produces enormous pressure change.

What the brain needs is perfusion pressure, which is mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure. The targets are intracranial pressure under about `22 mmHg` and cerebral perfusion pressure between `60` and `70 mmHg`. That equation explains why a single episode of hypotension is so damaging in head injury.

The Cushing reflex is the late warning: rising blood pressure, falling heart rate, and irregular breathing, as the body raises pressure to keep perfusing a squeezed brain. Uncal herniation pushes the temporal lobe against the third cranial nerve, giving a dilated pupil on the same side and weakness on the opposite side; tonsillar herniation compresses the brainstem and stops breathing.

> **Key:** The immediate measures are head of bed to `30` degrees with the neck straight, normal carbon dioxide rather than aggressive hyperventilation, avoiding hypotension and hypoxia at all costs, and hypertonic saline or mannitol to pull water out of brain tissue.
keyPoints: Alzheimer starts with memory, vascular declines in steps, Lewy body brings hallucinations and antipsychotic sensitivity, frontotemporal changes behavior first.
Parkinson symptoms appear only after 60-80% of substantia nigra neurons are lost; never interrupt levodopa or give dopamine blockers.
Multiple sclerosis is demyelination separated in space and time, worsened by heat, with oligoclonal bands in the spinal fluid.
Migraine is cortical spreading depression activating the trigeminovascular system and releasing CGRP, not a vascular spasm.
Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure; hypotension in head injury is as harmful as the pressure itself.

checks.q: An 80-year-old with fluctuating confusion and vivid visual hallucinations becomes agitated. Which medication is dangerous?
checks.why: Fluctuating cognition with detailed visual hallucinations suggests Lewy body dementia, where dopamine blockade can cause severe rigidity, autonomic instability, and death. Quetiapine is the usual alternative. Lorazepam has its own risks in the elderly but not this specific catastrophic sensitivity.

checks.q: A patient with a large intracranial hemorrhage has an intracranial pressure of 30 mmHg and a mean arterial pressure of 80 mmHg. What is the cerebral perfusion pressure and why does it matter?
choices: `50 mmHg`, which is below the target of 60-70 and risks ischemia
`30 mmHg`, equal to the intracranial pressure
It cannot be calculated without the intracranial volume
checks.why: Cerebral perfusion pressure is mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure, so 80 minus 30 is 50 mmHg. That is below the 60 to 70 mmHg target, meaning the brain is underperfused. This equation is also why hypotension is so damaging in head injury.

checks.q: A patient with multiple sclerosis reports that her old right leg weakness returns every time she takes a hot bath or runs a fever. What explains this?
choices: A new demyelinating lesion forms with each temperature rise
Heat further impairs conduction along already demyelinated axons
checks.why: Demyelinated axons conduct marginally, and raising temperature reduces conduction further, so old deficits reappear without new damage. This is why a febrile multiple sclerosis patient may look like a relapse but is not, and cooling plus treating the fever restores the baseline.

lessons.title: Renal and endocrine second pass: the glomerulus, the diabetic, and the thyroid
lessons.body:
## Two ways a glomerulus fails

The glomerulus is a filter with a charged, porous membrane. It can fail by becoming too leaky to protein, or by becoming inflamed and leaking blood. Those are the nephrotic and nephritic syndromes, and telling them apart is a single urine dipstick away.

| | Nephrotic | Nephritic |
|---|---|---|
| Core lesion | podocyte injury, filter leaks protein | glomerular inflammation, filter leaks blood |
| Urine | protein over `3.5 g/day`, frothy, bland sediment | red blood cells and **red cell casts**, mild protein |
| Blood pressure | normal or low | high |
| Volume | heavy edema, periorbital in the morning | oliguria and fluid retention |
| Classic causes | minimal change in children, focal segmental sclerosis, membranous, diabetic nephropathy, amyloid | post-streptococcal, IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, lupus nephritis |

Nephrotic syndrome has three consequences that follow from losing protein in the urine: low albumin causes edema, the liver compensates by making lipoproteins so cholesterol rises, and antithrombin III is lost in the urine so the patient clots, classically in the renal vein.

> **Key:** Red cell casts are made in the tubule and can only come from the glomerulus. Their presence means the bleeding is renal, not from a stone or the bladder, and it turns a hematuria workup into a nephrology emergency.

IgA nephropathy and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis are separated by timing. IgA nephropathy produces visible blood in the urine `1` to `2` days after a sore throat begins; post-streptococcal disease appears `1` to `3` weeks after the infection has resolved.

## What chronic glucose does to vessels

High glucose damages tissue through three linked pathways: glucose sticks irreversibly to proteins to form advanced glycation end products, excess glucose is shunted into sorbitol which draws water into nerve and lens, and protein kinase C activation thickens basement membranes.

**Microvascular** damage hits places with no autoregulation. Retinopathy progresses from microaneurysms to new fragile vessels that bleed. Nephropathy begins with hyperfiltration, then microalbuminuria, then overt proteinuria and falling filtration. Neuropathy starts in the longest nerves, giving a stocking-glove loss that lets a patient walk on a foreign body for days.

**Macrovascular** damage is accelerated atherosclerosis: heart attack, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease. Autonomic neuropathy means the heart attack can be silent, presenting as breathlessness, fatigue, or vomiting with no chest pain at all.

A diabetic foot ulcer is three failures at once: neuropathy removes the warning, arterial disease removes the healing, and impaired white cell function removes the defense.

## The thyroid at both ends

Thyroid hormone sets the metabolic rate of every cell. The pituitary releases TSH, the thyroid releases mostly T4, and tissues convert it to the active T3. Feedback means a **low TSH with high T4** is primary hyperthyroidism and a **high TSH with low T4** is primary hypothyroidism.

Graves disease is an antibody that stimulates the TSH receptor, adding a diffuse goiter and eye protrusion. A toxic nodule or thyroiditis produces the same hormone excess without the eye findings.

**Thyroid storm** is decompensated hyperthyroidism, almost always triggered by infection, surgery, trauma, or an iodine load. Fever above `38.5 C`, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation out of proportion to the fever, agitation or delirium, vomiting and diarrhea, and heart failure. Treatment blocks the pathway at four points: a beta blocker for the adrenergic storm, a thionamide to stop hormone synthesis, iodine given at least an hour after the thionamide to stop release, and steroids to block peripheral conversion.

> **Trap:** Iodine given before the thionamide feeds the gland fresh substrate and makes the storm worse. The order matters.

**Myxedema coma** is the opposite emergency: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation with carbon dioxide retention, hyponatremia, and depressed consciousness in an older patient in winter. Treatment is intravenous levothyroxine plus hydrocortisone, because unrecognized adrenal insufficiency alongside it is common and thyroid hormone alone can precipitate crisis.

## Adrenal failure

Primary adrenal insufficiency destroys the whole gland, so both cortisol and aldosterone are lost: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and skin darkening from the ACTH precursor. Secondary insufficiency, usually from abruptly stopping chronic steroids, spares aldosterone, so potassium stays normal and there is no hyperpigmentation. Either can decompensate into adrenal crisis under stress, and the treatment is hydrocortisone `100 mg` IV plus fluid and glucose.
keyPoints: Nephrotic leaks protein over 3.5 g/day with bland sediment; nephritic leaks blood with red cell casts and hypertension.
Nephrotic syndrome clots because antithrombin III is lost in the urine, classically causing renal vein thrombosis.
IgA nephropathy appears 1-2 days after a sore throat starts; post-streptococcal disease appears 1-3 weeks after it ends.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy makes myocardial infarction silent, presenting as breathlessness, fatigue, or vomiting.
In thyroid storm the thionamide must precede iodine by at least an hour, or the iodine fuels more hormone synthesis.

checks.q: A 30-year-old has cola-colored urine, a blood pressure of 168/96, and red blood cell casts on microscopy. Which category is this?
checks.why: Red cell casts, hematuria, and hypertension define a nephritic picture from glomerular inflammation. Nephrotic syndrome leaks protein with a bland sediment and normal or low pressure. Obstruction and pre-renal failure do not produce casts made of red cells.

checks.q: A patient in thyroid storm is ordered propranolol, methimazole, hydrocortisone, and potassium iodide. What sequencing rule applies?
choices: Iodide first to shrink the gland
Iodide at least 1 hour after the methimazole
Hydrocortisone must be held until the thyroid function tests return
The beta blocker is given last
checks.why: Iodine blocks hormone release but also supplies substrate for synthesis. Given before the thionamide it can worsen the storm, so it follows methimazole by at least an hour. Steroids are given early to block peripheral T4 to T3 conversion, and the beta blocker controls the adrenergic surge immediately.

checks.q: A patient has hypotension, sodium 126 mEq/L, potassium 5.8 mEq/L, and darkened skin creases. Which diagnosis fits?
choices: Secondary adrenal insufficiency from steroid withdrawal
checks.why: Loss of aldosterone as well as cortisol produces hyperkalemia with hyponatremia, and excess ACTH precursor causes hyperpigmentation, both pointing to primary disease. Secondary insufficiency spares aldosterone, so potassium is normal and the skin is not pigmented. SIADH causes hyponatremia with normal potassium and no hypotension.

lessons.title: Hematologic pathophysiology: anemia, marrow malignancy, and the coagulopathy of trauma
lessons.body:
## Anemia has exactly three mechanisms

Either the marrow is not making red cells, something is destroying them, or they are being lost. The reticulocyte count separates the first from the other two: a marrow that is trying hard sends out young cells, so a high reticulocyte count means destruction or bleeding, and a low one means a production problem.

Cell size then narrows it further.

| Size | Causes |
|---|---|
| Microcytic, MCV under `80` | iron deficiency, thalassemia, anemia of chronic disease, lead, sideroblastic |
| Normocytic | acute blood loss, hemolysis, chronic disease, chronic kidney disease from lost erythropoietin |
| Macrocytic, MCV over `100` | B12 and folate deficiency (megaloblastic), alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia |

Iron studies separate the two common microcytic causes. Iron deficiency shows a low ferritin, a high total iron binding capacity, and a low saturation, because the body is hunting for iron. Anemia of chronic disease shows a low serum iron with a low binding capacity and a normal or high ferritin, because inflammation is hiding iron away rather than lacking it.

Hemolysis has its own fingerprint: high LDH from spilled cell contents, high indirect bilirubin from broken-down heme, a **low haptoglobin** because that protein is consumed mopping up free hemoglobin, and a high reticulocyte count. A positive direct antiglobulin test means antibodies are coating the cells; a negative one points to mechanical destruction such as a heart valve or the microangiopathies.

> **Trap:** B12 and folate deficiency look identical on the blood count, with large cells and hypersegmented neutrophils. Only B12 deficiency damages the spinal cord, causing loss of vibration and position sense and an unsteady gait. Giving folate alone corrects the blood picture while the neurologic damage continues and becomes permanent.

## Leukemia and lymphoma

Leukemia is malignancy of blood-forming cells circulating in blood and marrow; lymphoma is malignancy of lymphocytes forming masses in nodes. Marrow packed with malignant cells fails at all three of its jobs at once, so patients present with anemia, infection from neutropenia, and bleeding from thrombocytopenia.

- **Acute lymphoblastic leukemia**: the most common childhood cancer, with bone pain, bruising, and adenopathy.
- **Acute myeloid leukemia**: adults; the promyelocytic subtype presents with disseminated intravascular coagulation.
- **Chronic lymphocytic leukemia**: older adults, frequently found incidentally as a high lymphocyte count with smudge cells.
- **Chronic myeloid leukemia**: the Philadelphia chromosome fuses `BCR` to `ABL`, and the drug imatinib was built to block exactly that fusion protein.
- **Hodgkin lymphoma**: Reed-Sternberg cells, spread to contiguous node groups, night sweats, weight loss, and fever.

A white count above `100,000` thickens blood enough to obstruct capillaries, producing headache, visual change, confusion, and breathlessness. That is leukostasis and it is an emergency.

## The coagulopathy of trauma

A bleeding trauma patient does not simply run out of clotting factors; the bleeding itself changes the clotting system.

1. **Tissue hypoperfusion** activates protein C, which switches off thrombin generation and releases the brake on fibrinolysis. Clots that do form are dissolved. This begins within minutes, before a single bag of fluid is given.
2. **Hypothermia** slows enzyme activity; every clotting factor works poorly below `35 C`, and a coagulation panel run at `37 C` hides this completely.
3. **Acidosis** further inhibits the clotting enzyme complexes. Hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy reinforce each other, which is the lethal triad.
4. **Dilution**: crystalloid replaces volume with fluid that carries no oxygen and no clotting factors, worsening everything above.

> **Key:** The treatment follows the mechanism. Give blood products in balanced ratios rather than crystalloid, give tranexamic acid within `3` hours to block the fibrinolysis, actively warm the patient, and replace calcium, because the citrate in stored blood binds it and calcium is required by the cascade at several steps.

Two microangiopathies round out the picture. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is missing the enzyme that trims von Willebrand factor, so platelets clump across small vessels, shearing red cells. Hemolytic uremic syndrome follows Shiga toxin, usually in a child after bloody diarrhea, and hits the kidney hardest. In both, platelet transfusion adds fuel to the fire and is avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding.
keyPoints: Reticulocyte count separates a production problem from destruction or loss; MCV then narrows the cause.
Iron deficiency has low ferritin and high binding capacity; chronic disease has normal or high ferritin with low binding capacity.
Hemolysis shows high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and reticulocytosis.
Folate alone corrects the blood count in B12 deficiency while spinal cord damage progresses and becomes permanent.
Trauma coagulopathy starts with hypoperfusion-driven fibrinolysis; treat with balanced blood products, tranexamic acid within 3 hours, warming, and calcium.

checks.q: A patient has an MCV of 112 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils, an unsteady gait, and reduced vibration sense. Which treatment is unsafe alone?
checks.why: Folate corrects the megaloblastic blood picture but does nothing for the spinal cord damage of B12 deficiency, which then progresses silently and becomes permanent. B12 is the correct treatment here. Iron would not address a macrocytic anemia at all.

checks.q: A hypothermic trauma patient at 33.5 C has a normal coagulation panel drawn at the laboratory. Why can this be misleading?
choices: The panel is run at 37 C, so it does not reflect enzyme performance at the patient's actual temperature
The panel measures platelets, not factors
checks.why: Coagulation assays are warmed to 37 C, so they report how the factors would perform at normal temperature, not how they are performing in a cold patient. Clotting enzyme activity falls markedly below 35 C, which is why active rewarming is a hemostatic intervention.

checks.q: A patient with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura has a platelet count of 18,000 and scattered petechiae without major bleeding. What should be avoided?
choices: Red cell transfusion for symptomatic anemia
checks.why: In TTP the platelets are being consumed by microvascular clotting driven by uncleaved von Willebrand factor, so transfused platelets add substrate and can worsen thrombosis. Plasma exchange is the definitive treatment, steroids are adjunctive, and red cells may be given for anemia.

lessons.title: Ten illness scripts: chest, abdomen, and the great vessels
lessons.body:
## How to use these

Each script fills the same five slots: who gets it, the mechanism, the presentation with its discriminating feature, the confirming test, and the first move. Read them as patterns rather than facts, and the next time a real patient matches the shape, the whole script will come back at once.

### ST-elevation myocardial infarction

Older smoker or diabetic. A vulnerable plaque ruptures and thrombus occludes a coronary artery completely, killing full-thickness muscle within hours. Pressure-like chest pain at rest with sweating, nausea, and radiation to jaw or arm; diabetics and women may have no chest pain at all. ECG shows ST elevation in contiguous leads. Aspirin `324 mg` chewed, then catheterization within `90` minutes.

### Aortic dissection

Hypertensive man in his sixties, or a young Marfan patient. A tear in the intima lets blood split the aortic wall along its length. Sudden tearing pain that is maximal at onset and moves to the back, sometimes with a pulse or blood pressure difference between arms, or a stroke, or new aortic regurgitation. CT angiography confirms. Control heart rate with esmolol first, then blood pressure; surgery for type A.

### Cardiac tamponade

After chest trauma, a dissection, cancer, or uremia. Fluid in the pericardium raises the pressure around the heart until the ventricles cannot fill. Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, and a pulse that weakens on inspiration. Bedside ultrasound shows the effusion and a collapsing right atrium. Pericardiocentesis.

### Tension pneumothorax

Trauma, a ventilated patient, or a tall thin young man. Air enters the pleural space through a one-way valve, pressure builds, and the vena cava kinks so blood cannot return. Severe breathlessness, absent breath sounds on one side, distended neck veins, hypotension, late tracheal shift. It is a clinical diagnosis. Needle decompression then a chest tube, before any x-ray.

### Community-acquired pneumonia

Any age; worse in the old, the smoker, and the immunosuppressed. Organisms fill alveoli with neutrophil exudate, creating a shunt. Fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, focal crackles, hypoxemia. Chest radiograph shows an infiltrate. Antibiotics matched to setting and severity, plus oxygen.

### Appendicitis

Teens to thirties. The lumen obstructs, pressure rises, the wall becomes ischemic and infected, and inflammation finally reaches the parietal peritoneum. Vague periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, low fever, and tenderness at McBurney point. CT or ultrasound confirms. Antibiotics and appendectomy.

### Acute cholecystitis

Middle-aged, often female and overweight. A stone lodges in the cystic duct, the gallbladder distends, and the wall becomes inflamed and infected. Constant right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal, fever, and arrest of inspiration when the examiner presses under the right ribs. Ultrasound shows stones, a thick wall, and fluid. Antibiotics, fluids, cholecystectomy.

### Acute pancreatitis

Gallstones or alcohol account for most cases. Digestive enzymes activate inside the gland and it begins to digest itself, leaking fluid into the retroperitoneum. Severe epigastric pain boring to the back, better sitting forward, with vomiting. Lipase three times the upper limit confirms. Aggressive fluid, analgesia, and treating the cause.

### Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm

Smoker over `65`. A dilated aorta tears, bleeding into the retroperitoneum. Sudden abdominal or flank pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass; frequently mistaken for renal colic in someone who has never had a stone. Bedside ultrasound or CT if stable. Immediate vascular surgery and blood, not crystalloid.

### Variceal upper gastrointestinal bleed

Cirrhotic patient. Portal hypertension forces blood through fragile submucosal veins that rupture. Large-volume vomiting of blood, black tarry stool, tachycardia and hypotension, with a hemoglobin that is normal at first because whole blood is lost. Endoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic. Blood products, octreotide, antibiotics, and urgent endoscopy.

> **Key:** Four of these ten are conditions where the classic error is treating the wrong organ: dissection mistaken for infarction, ruptured aneurysm mistaken for renal colic, tamponade mistaken for heart failure, and tension pneumothorax mistaken for asthma. The discriminating feature in each is in the script.
keyPoints: Every script has the same five slots: who, mechanism, presentation with a discriminator, confirming test, first move.
Tearing pain maximal at onset with a limb pulse difference is dissection; pressure building over minutes is infarction.
Tamponade and tension pneumothorax both give hypotension with distended neck veins, separated by breath sounds.
A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm in a smoker over 65 is regularly mislabeled as first-time renal colic.
In acute hemorrhage the initial hemoglobin is normal, because whole blood is lost in proportion.

checks.q: A 62-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, with a systolic blood pressure of 178 in the right arm and 140 in the left. What is the first drug goal?
choices: Heart rate control with esmolol before blood pressure reduction
checks.why: This is aortic dissection, and the aim is to reduce the shearing force on the wall, which depends on the rate of pressure rise as well as the pressure. Rate control comes first so that a vasodilator does not cause a reflex tachycardia. Thrombolysis and anticoagulation are catastrophic in dissection.

checks.q: A 68-year-old smoker has sudden left flank pain, a blood pressure of 88/54, and a pulsatile abdominal mass. The triage note says renal colic. What is the concern?
checks.why: First-time flank pain in an older smoker with hypotension and a pulsatile mass is a ruptured aneurysm until proven otherwise. Stones usually begin decades earlier and do not cause hypotension. The mislabel is common and the delay is fatal.

checks.q: Which finding separates tension pneumothorax from cardiac tamponade at the bedside?
choices: Unilaterally absent breath sounds with hyperresonance
checks.why: Both cause obstructive shock with hypotension, distended neck veins, and tachycardia. Only tension pneumothorax removes breath sounds on one side and makes that side hyperresonant; tamponade muffles heart sounds while the lungs stay clear.

lessons.title: Ten illness scripts: brain, hormones, and overwhelming infection
lessons.body:
## Ten more, same five slots

### Large-vessel ischemic stroke

Older patient with atrial fibrillation, hypertension, or diabetes. A clot occludes a cerebral artery, killing a core of tissue surrounded by a salvageable penumbra kept alive by collaterals. Sudden focal deficit maximal at onset when embolic: face droop, arm weakness, speech change, gaze deviation. Non-contrast CT excludes bleeding, then CT angiography finds the vessel. Thrombolysis within `4.5` hours and thrombectomy for a large-vessel occlusion.

### Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Adults `40` to `60`, more often women, sometimes with polycystic kidney disease. A berry aneurysm at a branch point ruptures into the space around the brain. Thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds, the worst of the patient's life, with neck stiffness and vomiting. Non-contrast CT within `6` hours is highly sensitive; lumbar puncture if later and still suspected. Blood pressure control, neurosurgery, and nimodipine for vasospasm.

### Bacterial meningitis

Any age; extremes of age and immunosuppression are at highest risk. Organisms multiply in cerebrospinal fluid and the cytokine response breaks the blood-brain barrier, swelling the brain. Fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status; a purpuric rash suggests meningococcus. Lumbar puncture shows thousands of neutrophils, low glucose, and high protein. Dexamethasone with the first dose, then ceftriaxone and vancomycin immediately.

### Diabetic ketoacidosis

Type 1 diabetes, often after infection or missed insulin. Without insulin, fat is burned to ketoacids while glucose spills into urine and drags out litres of water. Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, dehydration. Glucose above `250 mg/dL`, anion gap acidosis, ketones present. Fluids, potassium before insulin if it is under `3.3 mEq/L`, then an insulin infusion.

### Thyroid storm

Known or unrecognized hyperthyroidism plus a stressor such as infection or surgery. Massive thyroid hormone excess drives every tissue at once. Fever, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation out of proportion to the fever, agitation, vomiting, heart failure. Very low TSH with high free T4; the diagnosis is clinical and treatment precedes the result. Beta blocker, thionamide, iodine an hour later, steroids.

### Adrenal crisis

A patient on chronic steroids who stopped them, or known adrenal disease under stress. Cortisol is absent when demand is highest, so vascular tone and glucose collapse. Hypotension unresponsive to fluid, weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, low sodium, low glucose, and high potassium if the disease is primary. Random cortisol is low. Hydrocortisone `100 mg` IV without waiting for confirmation.

### Pyelonephritis and urosepsis

Women, pregnancy, diabetes, obstruction, catheters. Bacteria ascend from the bladder and invade kidney tissue, and an obstructed infected kidney seeds the bloodstream. Fever, rigors, flank pain, vomiting, with white blood cell casts. Urinalysis and culture, and imaging when obstruction is possible. Ceftriaxone, fluids, and urgent drainage if obstructed.

### Necrotizing fasciitis

Diabetic, immunosuppressed, or after a minor wound or injection. Infection spreads along fascia and thromboses perforating vessels, killing tissue from the inside out. Pain far beyond the appearance, skin that has become numb, rapid spread, crepitus, and systemic toxicity. Diagnosis is surgical exploration, not imaging. Operating room plus broad antibiotics with clindamycin.

### Sickle cell acute chest syndrome

Known sickle cell disease, often a few days into a pain crisis. Sickled cells occlude pulmonary vessels; infection, infarction, and fat embolism from marrow all contribute. Fever, chest pain, cough, hypoxia, and a **new** infiltrate on the chest radiograph. Oxygen, analgesia, antibiotics covering atypicals, and exchange transfusion when severe.

### Anaphylaxis

Any age, with a known or unknown trigger. IgE-crosslinked mast cells degranulate, dumping histamine and tryptase: vessels dilate and leak, airways constrict. Onset within minutes with two or more systems involved, most often hives plus airway swelling, wheeze, or hypotension. It is a clinical diagnosis. Epinephrine `0.3-0.5 mg` intramuscularly into the outer thigh, repeated every `5-15` minutes.

> **Trap:** Three of these are diagnosed and treated before any confirming test exists: adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, and anaphylaxis. Waiting for the laboratory in any of them is the error that kills the patient.
keyPoints: Thunderclap headache maximal within seconds is subarachnoid hemorrhage; CT within 6 hours is highly sensitive.
Adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, and anaphylaxis are all treated before any confirmatory test returns.
Acute chest syndrome requires a new infiltrate plus fever or hypoxia and is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease.
Necrotizing fasciitis is diagnosed in the operating room; imaging that looks reassuring does not exclude it.
In DKA, potassium under 3.3 mEq/L is replaced before insulin is started, or the level will crash further.

checks.q: A 46-year-old describes a headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds two hours ago, with vomiting and neck stiffness. The neurologic exam is normal. What is the next step?
choices: Discharge with migraine treatment since the exam is normal
Non-contrast CT head now, with lumbar puncture if the CT is negative and suspicion remains
checks.why: Thunderclap onset is subarachnoid hemorrhage until excluded, and a normal neurologic examination is common early. CT within 6 hours is highly sensitive; beyond that or when negative with high suspicion, lumbar puncture looks for xanthochromia. Neck stiffness here comes from blood irritating the meninges.

checks.q: A patient on prednisone for 2 years stopped it abruptly a week ago and now has hypotension that does not respond to 2 L of fluid, vomiting, and a glucose of 54 mg/dL. What is the immediate treatment?
choices: Wait for a cortisol and ACTH stimulation test
checks.why: Fluid-unresponsive hypotension with hypoglycemia after steroid withdrawal is adrenal crisis, and hydrocortisone is given immediately; a cortisol level can be drawn first but never delays treatment. Vasopressors work poorly without cortisol, and antibiotics treat a possible trigger but not the crisis.

checks.q: A 21-year-old with sickle cell disease admitted for a pain crisis now has a fever of 38.8 C, chest pain, a saturation of 89%, and a new left lower lobe infiltrate. What is the diagnosis?
checks.why: A new pulmonary infiltrate with fever or hypoxia during a sickle cell admission defines acute chest syndrome, the leading cause of death in this disease. It requires oxygen, antibiotics covering atypicals, analgesia, and often exchange transfusion. Aplastic crisis is a fall in reticulocytes without an infiltrate.

cards.front: How do oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes differ in how many hits they need?
cards.back: An oncogene is a gain of function, so one damaged copy is enough. A tumor suppressor is a loss of function, so both copies must be lost — which is why inherited tumor suppressor mutations run in families.

cards.front: Name three oncogenes and three tumor suppressor genes with their cancers.
cards.back: Oncogenes: `RAS` in colon and pancreas, `HER2` in breast, `BCR-ABL` in chronic myeloid leukemia. Tumor suppressors: `p53` broadly, `BRCA1` and `BRCA2` in breast and ovary, `APC` in colon.

cards.front: List the capabilities a cell must acquire to become malignant.
cards.back: Grow unprompted, ignore stop signals, resist apoptosis (usually by losing `p53`), reactivate telomerase, build blood supply through angiogenesis, evade immune detection, and invade through the basement membrane.

cards.front: What is the stepwise progression from normal tissue to invasive cancer?
cards.back: Normal, hyperplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in place, then invasion. Screening works because every step before invasion is reversible or curable — a polyp removed at colonoscopy is a cancer that never happens.

cards.front: Why does colon cancer spread to the liver and prostate cancer to bone?
cards.back: Metastasis follows drainage. The colon drains through the portal vein straight into the liver. Prostate drains through vertebral venous plexuses into the spine, producing dense bone-building lesions.

cards.front: What must iron deficiency anemia in a man or postmenopausal woman prompt?
cards.back: Colonoscopy. A right-sided colon cancer bleeds a small volume daily, which is invisible in the toilet but obvious in the ferritin. Treating with iron alone treats the number and misses the cause.

cards.front: Which paraneoplastic syndromes come from small cell versus squamous cell lung cancer?
cards.back: Small cell secretes antidiuretic hormone causing SIADH and hyponatremia, or ACTH causing Cushing syndrome, and triggers Lambert-Eaton syndrome. Squamous cell secretes PTH-related peptide causing hypercalcemia.

cards.front: How does pancreatic cancer classically present?
cards.back: Painless jaundice with a palpable, non-tender gallbladder, weight loss, and sometimes new-onset diabetes. Risk factors are smoking and chronic pancreatitis, and it is usually advanced when found.

cards.front: What is the difference between tumor grade and tumor stage?
cards.back: Grade is how abnormal the cells look microscopically. Stage is how far the disease has travelled, using TNM: tumor size, nodes, metastasis. Stage drives prognosis and treatment far more than grade does.

cards.front: What are central and peripheral tolerance?
cards.back: Central tolerance deletes self-reactive lymphocytes as they mature in the thymus and bone marrow. Peripheral tolerance catches escapees using regulatory T cells and by shutting down cells that see antigen without a danger signal.

cards.front: What is molecular mimicry, with two examples?
cards.back: A microbe carries a protein resembling a human one, so antibodies against the infection attack the body. Streptococcal M protein resembles cardiac myosin (rheumatic fever); Campylobacter sugars resemble nerve myelin (Guillain-Barre).

cards.front: Name the four hypersensitivity types with their mediator and timing.
cards.back: Type I, IgE on mast cells, minutes. Type II, antibody against a cell surface, hours to days. Type III, immune complexes deposited in tissue, days. Type IV, T cells with no antibody, `48-72` hours.

cards.front: Give two diseases for each hypersensitivity type.
cards.back: I: anaphylaxis, allergic asthma. II: immune thrombocytopenia, Graves disease. III: lupus, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. IV: contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test and most drug rashes.

cards.front: Which antibodies are sensitive and which are specific in lupus?
cards.back: Antinuclear antibody is sensitive but not specific — many healthy people have it. Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith are specific. Lupus nephritis drives most of the mortality.

cards.front: How do rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis differ in pattern?
cards.back: Rheumatoid: symmetric small joints, morning stiffness over an hour that improves with use, systemic features, anti-CCP antibodies, erosive pannus. Osteoarthritis: asymmetric, worse with use, brief stiffness, no systemic features.

cards.front: Why is Graves disease a type II hypersensitivity even though it causes overactivity?
cards.back: The antibody binds the TSH receptor and stimulates it instead of destroying the cell. Type II simply means an antibody directed at a cell surface; the consequence can be activation, blockade, or destruction.

cards.front: What is measured to decide intubation in myasthenic crisis, and why not pulse oximetry?
cards.back: Forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force. Neuromuscular failure is a pump problem: oxygen saturation stays normal until the patient is nearly apneic, so waiting for desaturation means waiting too long.

cards.front: Why are steroids started before the biopsy in giant cell arteritis?
cards.back: Vision loss from ischemic optic neuropathy can become permanent within hours, and the temporal artery biopsy stays informative for one to two weeks after steroids begin. Treating first costs nothing diagnostically.

cards.front: How do you recognize autosomal dominant versus autosomal recessive inheritance in a family?
cards.back: Dominant appears in every generation, affects half of offspring, and usually involves structural proteins. Recessive skips generations, appears among siblings of unaffected carriers, and usually involves enzymes.

cards.front: Which rule makes X-linked recessive inheritance recognizable?
cards.back: Males are affected, transmission is through unaffected carrier mothers, and it never passes father to son. Hemophilia A and B, G6PD deficiency, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy follow this pattern.

cards.front: What is the molecular defect in sickle cell disease and when does it cause trouble?
cards.back: A single amino acid swap at position `6` of beta-globin produces hemoglobin S, which polymerizes into rigid rods when deoxygenated. The cells become stiff and sticky, causing vaso-occlusion and chronic hemolysis.

cards.front: Why are sickle cell patients vulnerable to encapsulated organisms?
cards.back: Repeated splenic infarction leaves them functionally asplenic by early childhood, so pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, meningococcus, and Salmonella can cause overwhelming infection rapidly.

cards.front: Name the five sickle cell crises and what defines each.
cards.back: Vaso-occlusive (bone and chest pain), acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate plus fever or hypoxia), splenic sequestration (sudden anemia with a large spleen), aplastic (parvovirus B19, reticulocytes fall to zero), and stroke.

cards.front: Why is fever in sickle cell disease treated as an emergency?
cards.back: Functional asplenia allows overwhelming sepsis within hours from encapsulated organisms. Blood cultures and a third-generation cephalosporin come first; a well appearance and normal white count do not exclude early bacteremia.

cards.front: What is the coagulation profile of hemophilia, and what is the head-injury rule?
cards.back: Prolonged PTT with a normal PT and normal platelet count, causing deep joint and muscle bleeds. With a head injury, factor replacement goes in before the CT, because imaging does not change the treatment and delay does.

cards.front: What are the emergency consequences of Marfan syndrome?
cards.back: Fibrillin-1 mutation weakens connective tissue, so the aortic root dilates and tears — type A dissection decades earlier than expected — and the lung blebs rupture, causing spontaneous pneumothorax.

cards.front: What story suggests congenital long QT syndrome?
cards.back: Syncope or sudden death during exertion, strong emotion, or a startling noise such as an alarm, plus a family history of young sudden death or drowning. Torsades is the arrhythmia; treatment is avoiding QT drugs, beta blockade, and often a defibrillator.

cards.front: How do G6PD deficiency and hereditary angioedema each present?
cards.back: G6PD: sudden hemolysis with bite cells after sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, or fava beans. Hereditary angioedema: bradykinin-driven swelling of face, airway, or bowel with no hives and no response to epinephrine or steroids.

cards.front: Why does lobar pneumonia cause hypoxemia that oxygen only partly fixes?
cards.back: Alveoli fill with neutrophil exudate, so that lung is perfused but not ventilated. That is a shunt, and blood passing through it never meets the supplemental oxygen being delivered.

cards.front: How do typical and atypical pneumonia differ mechanically?
cards.back: Typical pneumonia (pneumococcus) fills alveoli with pus, giving lobar consolidation and rusty sputum. Atypical pneumonia inflames the interstitium, giving a dry cough, a patient who looks better than the film, and no cell wall for beta-lactams to attack.

cards.front: What proves a urinary infection is in the kidney rather than the bladder?
cards.back: White blood cell casts, which are formed in the renal tubule and can only come from kidney tissue, alongside fever, flank pain, and vomiting.

cards.front: Why is an obstructed, infected kidney an emergency?
cards.back: The obstruction creates a closed, pressurized abscess that antibiotics cannot sterilize, and pressure forces bacteria into the bloodstream. Drainage by stent or nephrostomy is the treatment; the antibiotic is support.

cards.front: Give the cerebrospinal fluid pattern for bacterial versus viral meningitis.
cards.back: Bacterial: high opening pressure, thousands of neutrophils, glucose under two thirds of serum, high protein. Viral: normal pressure, tens to hundreds of lymphocytes, normal glucose, normal or mildly high protein.

cards.front: Explain why dexamethasone must precede the first antibiotic in meningitis.
cards.back: Killing bacteria releases cell wall fragments that intensify the cytokine response injuring the brain. Blunting that burst reduces hearing loss and death. Given afterward, the surge has already happened.

cards.front: How does infective endocarditis actually begin?
cards.back: Turbulent flow strips valve endothelium, so platelets and fibrin form a sterile clot there. Passing bacteria stick to and grow inside that clot, shielded from neutrophils by fibrin — which is why treatment takes weeks of IV antibiotics.

cards.front: Distinguish Janeway lesions from Osler nodes.
cards.back: Janeway lesions are painless flat spots on palms and soles caused by septic emboli. Osler nodes are painful raised lesions on fingers and toes caused by immune complex deposition. Painless is embolic, painful is immune.

cards.front: Why does necrotizing fasciitis cause numb skin and pain out of proportion?
cards.back: Infection spreads along the fascial plane and thromboses the small vessels perforating up to the skin. The deep tissue and cutaneous nerves die while the skin still looks nearly normal, producing anesthesia over intense pain.

cards.front: Match each dementia to its recognizable pattern: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal.
cards.back: Alzheimer: gradual memory loss first. Vascular: stepwise decline with focal deficits. Lewy body: fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, antipsychotic sensitivity. Frontotemporal: personality and behavior change first, often before `65`.

cards.front: Why is haloperidol dangerous in Lewy body dementia?
cards.back: These patients have severe neuroleptic sensitivity: dopamine blockade can cause profound rigidity, autonomic instability, and death. Quetiapine is the usual alternative when an antipsychotic is unavoidable.

cards.front: How do you distinguish delirium from dementia at the bedside?
cards.back: Delirium is acute in onset, fluctuates within hours, and features inattention; it is almost always caused by something outside the brain. Dementia is slow and stable from hour to hour.

cards.front: What is lost in Parkinson disease, and how much before symptoms appear?
cards.back: Dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, containing alpha-synuclein clumps called Lewy bodies. Symptoms begin only after roughly `60%` to `80%` of those neurons are gone.

cards.front: Name two medication rules in Parkinson disease.
cards.back: Never interrupt levodopa-carbidopa — abrupt withdrawal causes a rigidity and fever syndrome resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome. And avoid dopamine blockers such as metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, and haloperidol; use ondansetron and quetiapine instead.

cards.front: Name four characteristic findings in multiple sclerosis.
cards.back: Optic neuritis with painful vision loss, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, an electric shock down the spine on neck flexion, and worsening of old deficits with heat. MRI shows plaques and spinal fluid shows oligoclonal bands.

cards.front: What is the current mechanism of migraine?
cards.back: A slow wave of cortical depolarization then suppression spreads at about `3 mm` per minute, matching the speed of visual aura, and activates trigeminal endings that release CGRP, causing neurogenic inflammation and vasodilation.

cards.front: Why does intracranial pressure stay flat and then rise suddenly as a bleed grows?
cards.back: The skull holds a fixed volume, and cerebrospinal fluid and venous blood are displaced first. Once those buffers are spent the compliance curve turns vertical, so a small additional volume produces an enormous pressure rise.

cards.front: Give the cerebral perfusion pressure equation, its targets, and the immediate measures for high intracranial pressure.
cards.back: Perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure; targets are ICP under about `22 mmHg` and CPP `60-70 mmHg`. Head up `30` degrees, neck straight, normal carbon dioxide, no hypotension or hypoxia, hypertonic saline or mannitol.

cards.front: Contrast nephrotic and nephritic syndrome in one line each.
cards.back: Nephrotic is podocyte injury leaking protein over `3.5 g/day` with heavy edema and bland sediment. Nephritic is glomerular inflammation leaking blood, with red cell casts, hypertension, and oliguria.

cards.front: Why do nephrotic patients clot?
cards.back: Antithrombin III is small enough to be lost through the leaking glomerulus, so a natural anticoagulant is excreted in the urine. Renal vein thrombosis is the classic result.

cards.front: What does a red blood cell cast tell you, and why?
cards.back: That the bleeding is glomerular. Casts are moulded in the renal tubule, so red cells inside one must have entered upstream in the glomerulus rather than from a stone, tumor, or the bladder.

cards.front: How does timing separate IgA nephropathy from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
cards.back: IgA nephropathy produces visible blood in the urine `1-2` days after a sore throat starts. Post-streptococcal disease appears `1-3` weeks after the infection has resolved.

cards.front: Name the three biochemical pathways by which high glucose damages tissue.
cards.back: Advanced glycation end products form when glucose sticks irreversibly to proteins; excess glucose is shunted into sorbitol, drawing water into nerve and lens; and protein kinase C activation thickens basement membranes.

cards.front: Why can a diabetic have a heart attack with no chest pain?
cards.back: Autonomic neuropathy damages the visceral afferent nerves that carry cardiac pain, so infarction presents instead as breathlessness, fatigue, sweating, confusion, or vomiting.

cards.front: Which three failures combine to produce a diabetic foot ulcer?
cards.back: Neuropathy removes the warning of injury, peripheral arterial disease removes the blood supply needed to heal, and impaired white cell function removes the defense against infection.

cards.front: Name the four treatment targets in thyroid storm and the sequencing rule.
cards.back: Beta blocker for the adrenergic storm, thionamide to stop synthesis, iodine at least an hour later to stop release, and steroids to block peripheral conversion. Iodine before the thionamide supplies substrate and worsens the storm.

cards.front: How do primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency differ, and what is the emergency treatment?
cards.back: Primary loses cortisol and aldosterone: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hyperpigmentation. Secondary spares aldosterone, so potassium is normal and there is no pigmentation. Crisis is treated with hydrocortisone `100 mg` IV plus fluid and glucose.

cards.front: What are the three mechanisms of anemia, and which test separates them?
cards.back: Underproduction, destruction, and loss. The reticulocyte count separates them: a high count means the marrow is responding to destruction or bleeding, a low count means a production problem.

cards.front: Sort anemia causes by cell size.
cards.back: Microcytic: iron deficiency, thalassemia, chronic disease, lead, sideroblastic. Normocytic: acute blood loss, hemolysis, chronic disease, chronic kidney disease. Macrocytic: B12 and folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia.

cards.front: How do iron studies separate iron deficiency from anemia of chronic disease?
cards.back: Iron deficiency: low ferritin, high total iron binding capacity, low saturation — the body is hunting for iron. Chronic disease: low serum iron, low binding capacity, normal or high ferritin — iron is being hidden, not missing.

cards.front: What is the laboratory fingerprint of hemolysis?
cards.back: High LDH from spilled cell contents, high indirect bilirubin from broken-down heme, low haptoglobin because it is consumed mopping up free hemoglobin, and a high reticulocyte count.

cards.front: Why is giving folate alone dangerous in an untyped megaloblastic anemia?
cards.back: B12 and folate deficiency look identical on the blood count. Folate corrects the cells while B12-related spinal cord degeneration continues, causing permanent loss of vibration sense, position sense, and gait.

cards.front: Distinguish leukemia from lymphoma, and name the four main leukemias.
cards.back: Leukemia is malignancy of blood-forming cells in blood and marrow; lymphoma forms masses in nodes. ALL in children, AML in adults, CLL in older adults with smudge cells, CML with the Philadelphia chromosome treated by imatinib.
